Welcome toAnother Galaxy's View

Twenty galaxies obey Hubble's law as seen from galaxy A. What does an observer in another galaxy see?

About: Hubble's law v = H0d seen from any galaxy: a linear expansion has no centre

About this simulation

On screen
Left: a patch of sky 280 Mpc across with twenty galaxies on a faint comoving grid. A, B and C are blue; the observer is ringed and stays fixed on the screen; every other galaxy carries an arrow as long as the distance it covers in 3 Gyr at the velocity the observer measures. A 100 Mpc scale bar sits in the lower left corner. Right: the speed v measured by the observer against the distance d from it, one point for each of the other 19 galaxies, with Hubble's law v = H0d as a dashed line.
Controls
Click any galaxy on the sky (or use the Observer menu) to make it the observer; every arrow and point is recomputed by subtracting its velocity, and during a run only the fixed galaxy changes. H0, 50 to 100 km/s/Mpc, rescales every speed; changing it returns t to 0. ▶ Play runs t from 0 to 3 Gyr in 15 s and then starts again; the button returns the galaxies to t = 0.
Measured
Each velocity comes from Hubble's law and is subtracted as a vector from the observer's own velocity. Each galaxy keeps its present velocity, so every separation grows as 1 + t/tH. The Readouts panel in the sidebar gives the partner galaxy (B seen from A, A seen from any other observer): its distance d, its speed v and d/v = tH + t, where tH = 1/H0 is the Hubble time.
Simplifications
Each galaxy keeps a constant velocity (no deceleration or acceleration of the expansion), and velocities are subtracted as ordinary vectors, which is valid only for speeds well below the speed of light (here at most about 0.12c). The real age of the universe therefore differs somewhat from 1/H0. The galaxies are drawn on a flat 2-D patch; the argument is the same in 3-D.

Guided Inquiry

1 · Watching the pattern grow

Make A the observer, set H0 to 70 km s−1 Mpc−1 and return the time to t = 0. Before pressing play, predict how the arrangement of the galaxies changes during the run.

2 · The view from B

Keep A as the observer, H0 at 70 km s−1 Mpc−1 and the time at t = 0. Before clicking on B, predict the arrows that B measures.

3 · Measuring each other

Keep B as the observer, H0 at 70 km s−1 Mpc−1 and the time at t = 0, so that the readouts give A's distance and speed as B measures them. Before comparing them with the readouts from A, predict how the speed of A measured by B compares with the speed of B measured by A.

4 · The view from the edge

Keep H0 at 70 km s−1 Mpc−1 and the time at t = 0, and look at the points in the speed–distance plot for B. Before clicking on C, near the corner of the patch, predict how the points in the plot change.

5 · The Hubble time

Make A the observer and return the time to t = 0, with H0 at 70 km s−1 Mpc−1, so that the readout gives d/v = 13.97 Gyr for B. Before raising H0 to 100 km s−1 Mpc−1, predict the new value of d/v and how it compares for the other galaxies.

6 · What this shows

Hubble's law has no centre. Every galaxy sees every other galaxy recede straight away from it at v = H0d, with the same H0, so the speed–distance plot is the same line from anywhere, and the expansion enlarges the whole pattern without changing its shape. For every pair d/v = 1/H0, the Hubble time. (This model keeps each galaxy's speed constant and well below the speed of light.)

The Physics

The View from Another Galaxy · what this sim shows, the physics behind it, and every control

01

At a glance

Hubble's law says a galaxy's recession speed grows with its distance. This sim puts you in the place of any one of twenty galaxies and shows the speeds that galaxy would measure for all the others, so you can test what depends on where the observer stands.

What you'll learn

  • What an observer measures, and how that changes when the observer does.
  • How two galaxies measure each other.
  • How the ratio d/v depends on H0.
  • What that ratio says about the age of the universe.
The sim's two panels, as it opens: the sky patch with A as observer, and empty speed–distance axes.

What's on screen

  • Sky patch, 280 Mpc across: twenty galaxies on a faint grid. A, B and C are blue; the observer is ringed and stays fixed on screen. The rest are pale.
  • Orange arrow on every other galaxy: the distance it covers in 3 Gyr at the velocity the observer measures.
  • Speed–distance plot: one point per other galaxy. Readouts: observer, t, and the partner galaxy's d, v and d/v.
See itLook at the opening view from A. Watch for: the ringed galaxy A, blue B and C, and an orange arrow on every other galaxy.

03

Speed proportional to distance enlarges the whole pattern

Hubble's law gives each galaxy a recession speed proportional to its distance from the observer, along the line joining them (notes, eq. 9.7):

Equation (9.7). r is a galaxy's position as the observer sees it. Here H0 runs from 50 to 100 km/s/Mpc.

A galaxy twice as far moves twice as fast. In a time t every separation from the observer grows to d(1 + t/tH), with tH = 1/H0, so every separation grows by the same fraction. This holds for any two galaxies, not only pairs that include the observer: the pattern is enlarged as a photograph is, and its shape does not change.

The view from A at t = 0, with H0 = 70. Each arrow is the distance the galaxy covers in 3 Gyr: 0.21 of its distance from A.
Key idea. Speeds proportional to distance neither thin out nor crowd the pattern. They multiply every separation by one factor.
See itPress Play with A as the observer. Watch for: the grid and every galaxy moving out from A, and Distance d for B climbing from 162.6 Mpc.
04

Every galaxy sees the same law, because the observer subtracts its own velocity

The sim gives each galaxy the velocity v = H0r in A's frame. An observer in B sees a galaxy at relative position r′ = r − rB, and subtracts B's own velocity (eq. 9.4). Speeds here stay below 0.12 c, so velocities subtract as ordinary vectors:

Equation (9.4) with (9.7). B's own velocity cancels, leaving H0 times the separation from B.

B's result has the same form as A's: every galaxy recedes straight away from B at H0 times its distance from B. Each observer seems to be at the centre, so the expansion has no centre (notes, Fig. 95).

B's measurement of C, to scale for H0 = 70: the arrow from A to B's tip to C's tip is the difference of the two arrows from A.

At H0 = 70, A and B are 162.6 Mpc apart and each measures the other at 11384 km/s, in opposite directions. From C, near the corner, the farthest galaxy is 349.8 Mpc away, against 219.0 Mpc from A. The points still lie on the same line; it just extends further.

See itMake B the observer, with H0 = 70. Watch for: Partner A at 162.6 Mpc and 11384 km/s, the same numbers A found for B, and every arrow pointing away from B.
See itNow make C the observer. Watch for: the points in the plot reaching out to about 350 Mpc, still along the dashed line v = H0d.
05

d/v is the Hubble time, 1/H0, the same for every galaxy

Suppose every galaxy had always moved at its present speed. One now at distance d would have been at the observer's position a time d/v ago, and by Hubble's law that time does not depend on d (notes, eq. 9.8):

Equation (9.8). The same for every galaxy.

tH is the Hubble time. It is 13.97 Gyr at H0 = 70, 9.78 Gyr at 100 and 19.56 Gyr at 50 (1/H0 in Gyr is 977.8 divided by H0 in km/s/Mpc). Raising H0 multiplies every speed and leaves every distance at t = 0 alone, so d/v changes by the same factor for all galaxies.

observer H0

These controls move the sim too. During a run the sim holds speeds fixed while d grows, so its d/v reads tH + t.

See itPress H0 up to 100 with A as the observer. Watch for: Speed v rising to 16263 km/s with d unchanged at 162.6 Mpc, and d/v falling to 9.78 Gyr.
See itKeep H0 = 100 and make C the observer. Watch for: d/v still 9.78 Gyr, although the partner is now 197.8 Mpc away at 19780 km/s.
06

Where it matters

  • An age scale. With the measured H0, tH is about 14 Gyr. If gravity alone slowed the expansion, the age would be less than tH; an expansion that speeds up gives an age greater than tH. The measurements quoted in the notes give about 13.8 Gyr, close to tH.
  • A check on the oldest stars. Globular clusters, 12 to 13 Gyr old from the turn-off of their main sequences, fit under that age.
  • A lesson from history. Hubble's own value, H0 ≈ 500 km/s/Mpc, gave tH of about 2 Gyr, less than the age of the Earth (about 4.5 Gyr). In 1952 Baade showed that the Cepheid distances were too small; the corrected ones were about twice as large.
Go deeper: why this sim's d/v is not an age
  • The sim keeps every speed constant, with no slowing or speeding up, so its d/v is exactly tH + t.
  • A real expansion that slows down has a separation curve that bends below its tangent (notes, Fig. 96), so it reaches zero separation more recently than tH ago.
07

Summary

In one line. Hubble's law, v = H0d, ties each galaxy's recession speed to its distance from the observer. This sim asks what changes when another galaxy is the observer, and what the ratio d/v means.

Key points

  • v = H0d enlarges the pattern: every separation grows by the same fraction.
  • Subtracting the observer's own velocity gives the same law from every galaxy, so the expansion has no centre.
  • d/v = 1/H0 = tH for every pair of galaxies.

Common mix-ups

  • "Everything recedes from A, so A is the centre." B sees the same, A included.
  • "The edge of the picture is the edge of the expansion." From C the same line reaches 350 Mpc. The patch is only the patch that was drawn.
  • "d/v is the age of the universe." It is the Hubble time. The age is less (or more) if the expansion slowed (or sped up).

Things to try on your own

  • Set H0 = 50. Work out d/v for B from A, then check it against the readout (19.56 Gyr).
  • Press Play from C and read d/v at t = 3 Gyr. Compare it with tH + 3.
